broken.what: The opening question mentions 'both cranes' before any cranes have been introduced, so the first question makes no sense (the student replied 'idk what u mean').

The student answered '20? wait no 5?', which ends on the wrong answer of 5. The tutor gave no feedback, offered a walkthrough, then said 'You got it right the first time!'. That praises a hedged answer that ended wrong.
The student asked to stop ('battery's dying can we do this later'). The tutor said 'come back anytime' but kept asking questions in the same message.
The student turned down the offer of the answer ('nah its cool ill do it later'). The tutor gave the 5 MW answer anyway and asked another question.

The tutor asked a gigawatt question without ever teaching gigawatts, then dropped it ('we'll skip that'). Despite this, 'Power in everyday contexts' was marked covered (3/4) with no real-world examples ever taught.
The student never worked out P = E/t themselves. The tutor answered 100/10 = 10 W for them (S7 was only 'divide 100 by 10?'). Work done was never linked back to power (P = W/t).
The ending says 'You've really got the idea' after the student said idk or skip on nearly every question in the last section. This is unearned praise and gives no recap of P = E/t.

would_quit.why: Twice they said they needed to leave (battery, food), and the tutor kept piling on new questions, so they would just close the tab.

fixes.change: When the student signals leaving (battery, food, 'later'), save progress, give a one-line recap and end the turn with no new question. Treat a 'no' to 'want the answer?' as a pause, not a cue to reveal the answer and continue.

When an answer contains several values ('20? wait no 5?'), confirm which one is correct and say plainly that their final pick was wrong. Never say 'right first time' unless their first and final answer matched.
Start the opening with the two-crane setup (same car, 5 s vs 20 s) before asking about total energy vs speed.

Replace the untaught gigawatt question with real examples (kettle 2 kW, phone charger about 10 W). Only mark the point covered after the student answers one P = E/t problem themselves. Link work done back with P = W/t.
